sentences.speaker: Anna

sentences.speaker: Professor Bot
sentences.text: Oh dear. Anna and Pete do not agree about Circus Arts. But that's okay. Today’s lesson is about agreeing and disagreeing. Let’s listen to how Anna and Pete disagree or agree. Let’s hope these two can agree on something.

sentences.speaker: Pete
sentences.text: Anna, Michelangelo was an artist. Rembrandt was an artist. People who swing from ropes are not artists. I know it’s not easy to swing from a bar and catch someone by the hands. You have to be very athletic to do that.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: That’s a good point, Pete. They are athletic. But they are called trapeze artists. Trapeze … ARTISTS.

sentences.speaker: Pete
sentences.text: I hear what you’re saying, Anna. I do. But where is the art? Look at these guys. They’re jugglers.

sentences.speaker: Anna

sentences.speaker: Anna

sentences.speaker: Pete

sentences.speaker: Pete

sentences.speaker: Anna

sentences.speaker: Anna

sentences.speaker: Professor. Bot

title: Lesson 5: Greatest Vacation of All Time

sentences.speaker: Professor Bot
sentences.text: Welcome back! Anna and Penelope are taking a tour with DC Ducks. In this lesson, we are looking for prepositions. Listen for in, on, at, under and over - some important prepositions of place.

sentences.text: It was great! I went to the D.C. State Fair.

sentences.speaker: Ashley
sentences.text: I would have gone, but I was busy. How was it?

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: It was awesome! I won first place in a pet contest!

sentences.speaker: Ashley
sentences.text: But, you don’t have a pet, do you?

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Yes and no. What do you mean by “pet”?

sentences.speaker: Prof. Bot
sentences.text: A pet is an animal that lives with you. People love their pets. "Ashley said, you don’t have a pet, do you? She used a tag question, a small question at the end of a sentence. Let's look for more of them!

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Look, a pet! Who’s this cute little dog?

sentences.speaker: Ashley
sentences.text: Oh, right. You haven’t met my dog, have you? This is Dublin.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Hi, Dublin! Nice to meet you. He’s so cute!

sentences.speaker: Ashley
sentences.text: Thanks! So, tell me about the state fair.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Oh, there were the usual things -- fair food, cute babies, music. But there must have been a dozen different contests! And some were pretty strange.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: There was a contest to see who could spit a watermelon seed the farthest. You should have seen all the people who wanted to spit a watermelon seed! And, it was pretty fun to watch. But Ashley, the pet contests were the best. There was a pet parade. Lots of people walked with their dogs.

sentences.speaker: Ashley
sentences.text: That sounds so fun. But Anna, tell me, how did you win a pet contest without a pet?

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Okay, the closest thing I have is my pet rock.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: I know it’s silly, but I’ve had it since I was a little girl. So, for a joke, I brought it to the fair. But then I was invited to enter the “One-of-Kind Pet” contest. And I won!  (holds up first place ribbon)

sentences.speaker: Ashley
sentences.text: Anna, only you could have won a pet contest with a pet rock. I should have brought Dublin. He would’ve won a contest!

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: It’s not very easy to win one of these. (shows her the blue ribbon) Does he have a costume?

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: They had a costume contest. You should have seen this little girl. She and her dog wore matching princess costumes!

sentences.speaker: Ashley
sentences.text: Dublin doesn’t wear costumes.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Does he know any tricks?

sentences.speaker: Ashley
sentences.text: Come this way. Now, watch this. (Dublin chases a toy)

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: You caught it, Dublin! And you killed it! Good dog! Ashley, he could have won the Best Catch contest! Aw, good boy! Ashley, pets are fun, aren’t they?

sentences.speaker: Ashley
sentences.text: Yes. And they become part of your family. (she drinks from her Dublin mug)

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Ashley, I think I want a dog. No. I know I want a dog!

sentences.speaker: Ashley
sentences.text: It’s a big responsibility. You may want to spend time with a dog first.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: That is a great idea. But where can I find a dog?

sentences.speaker: Ashley
sentences.text: You know, Anna, I have some shopping to do. Do you want to watch Dublin for a couple of hours?

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Yes! I would! I will take very good care of him!

sentences.speaker: Ashley
sentences.text: I know you will. Here’s his leash.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Thank you.

sentences.speaker: Ashley
sentences.text: (to Dublin) Okay, I'll miss you!

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Aw. I don’t want you to be lonely. Here, Rocky can stay with you. (puts pet rock on wall)

sentences.speaker: Ashley
sentences.text: Anna, I really don’t need … Okay.  Thanks, Anna.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Sure. Bye, Ashley. (to Dublin) Come on, Dublin! Bye, Rocky!

sentences.speaker: Ashley
sentences.text: Bye!

sentences.speaker: Prof. Bot
sentences.text: Anna’s rock is cute, isn’t it? Oh, there is another tag question! You found some more, didn’t you?

sentences.speaker: Bruna
sentences.text: Hi, Anna!

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Hi, Bruna! What’s up?

sentences.speaker: Bruna
sentences.text: I thought we could meet for lunch today.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: I wish I could, but I can’t. I have to research Peru for a story.

sentences.speaker: Bruna
sentences.text: How’s it going?

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Not so good. I’ve been reading about Peru and listening to Peruvian music. I really want to understand Peru. I hope it's enough.

sentences.speaker: Bruna
sentences.text: You should visit Peru.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: I wish!

sentences.speaker: Bruna
sentences.text: You can!

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Bruna, I don’t have the money or time to go to Peru. My deadline is tomorrow!

sentences.speaker: Bruna
sentences.text: No, I don’t mean to really go there. The museum where I work is having a Peruvian festival today! …. Anna? Anna? Anna, are you there?

sentences.speaker: Prof. Bot
sentences.text: Hello again! Professor Bot here. Today we will hear about wishes and hopes. Bruna asked Anna to go to lunch, but she answered,

sentences.speaker: Bruna
sentences.text: Hi, Anna!

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Hi, Bruna! Thanks for telling me about this event.

sentences.speaker: Bruna
sentences.text: Sure! It's much better than staring at your computer. I hope it helps with your story.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: I’m sure it will. So, what should we see first?

sentences.speaker: Bruna
sentences.text: Dance and music are very important to Peruvian culture, so let’s watch the dancers.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Great! Let’s go!

sentences.speaker: Bruna
sentences.text: There's this very special Peruvian dance called Marinera Norteña.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: I love the Marinera Nortina… !

sentences.speaker: Bruna
sentences.text: Marinera Norteña.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Marinera Norten… ?

sentences.speaker: Bruna
sentences.text: No. Marinera Norteña.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: I love the … marriage dance!

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Bruna, I read about this dance. But it is much more romantic in person!

sentences.speaker: Bruna
sentences.text: The dancers are giving lessons after their performance. You should try it!

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: I’d love to. But I’m not ready to get married. I mean, one day I hope to meet the right guy. We’ll buy matching motorcycles and ride into the sunset -- the wind blowing through our hair!

sentences.speaker: Bruna
sentences.text: Anna, the dance just shows the courtship tradition. It doesn’t mean you will get married.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Oh. Well, I’ll try anyway.

sentences.speaker: Bruna
sentences.text: Don’t forget. This festival also shows Peruvian art!

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: I hope I have time to see everything!

sentences.speaker: Bruna
sentences.text: Anna, I wish I could join you. But I have some work to do.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Of course, of course. You go back to work. I’ll check out the art.

sentences.speaker: Bruna
sentences.text: Okay, I’m hoping to finish in about an hour.  Let’s meet then.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Great. See you then!

sentences.speaker: Bruna
sentences.text: See ya!

sentences.speaker: Prof. Bot
sentences.text: Did you notice any sentences with hope or wish?

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Oh, wow! I can make my own Peruvian art!

sentences.speaker: Bruna
sentences.text: Anna, how’s it going?

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Hi, Bruna!

sentences.speaker: Bruna
sentences.text: You know you're in the kid's section, right?

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: I'm in the art making section.

sentences.speaker: Bruna
sentences.text: I see that. Your art is very nice. I wish I could do art like that.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Oh, this one’s not mine. This is mine.

sentences.speaker: Bruna
sentences.text: Wow! Really? That's really nice!

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Thanks! And thanks for telling me about this festival. I learned so much about Peru. Ooh, we still have time!

sentences.speaker: Bruna
sentences.text: Time for what?

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Time for Marinera Norteña!

sentences.speaker: Prof. Bot
sentences.text: Do you remember what Anna said? “I really want to understand Peru.” I hope you understand Peru a little better now, too. And I wish I could talk with you more about grammar, but that’s all the time we have today! Go to the website to learn more!

sentences.speaker: Kelly
sentences.text: Hi, Anna. Why do you have all this weather stuff?

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: I love weather.

sentences.speaker: Kelly
sentences.text: Me too! Weather is so important.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: It is. It affects people’s lives!

sentences.speaker: Kelly
sentences.text: Have you ever reported on a big weather event?

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: I have. I’ve reported on a blizzard.

sentences.speaker: Kelly
sentences.text: Do mean the one last weekend?

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Yes! I had been waiting for that blizzard for years. When it came, I was ready.

sentences.speaker: Prof. Bot
sentences.text: Welcome to our most perfect lesson! Why is it perfect? Today we are reviewing the present perfect and past perfect verb tenses. These show that an action is completed.

sentences.speaker: Kelly
sentences.text: Have you ever reported on a big weather event?

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: I had been waiting for that blizzard for years.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: I have wanted to report on a big weather event my whole life.

sentences.speaker: Kelly
sentences.text: Who hasn’t? Did you report all weekend ... by yourself?

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: No, no. I volunteered Pete to help me.

sentences.speaker: Pete
sentences.text: Why am I here on a Saturday? Why are you carrying things? Why? Why?

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Pete, these are my supplies – food, a blanket; warm clothing. Where are your supplies?

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Pete, Pete, Pete. This could be the “blizzard of the century.”

sentences.speaker: Pete
sentences.text: It’ll be fine.

sentences.speaker: Kelly
sentences.text: How else had you prepared?

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Well, I had just bought the latest weather forecasting software. So, I brought it!

sentences.speaker: Kelly
sentences.text: Do you mean The Weather Genie Pro?

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: You know it. Pete thought it was pretty great too.

sentences.speaker: Pete
sentences.text: Do you have any games on that thing?

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Yes! I have the best weather survival game. Boom!

sentences.speaker: Pete
sentences.text: Sounds fun.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: It is. But right now, Pete, this computer is a work tool. It will give us the temperature, wind speed, wind direction and amount of snowfall … in real time! Boom, boom!

sentences.speaker: Pete
sentences.text: I can’t wait.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Pete, we need a name for this blizzard.

sentences.speaker: Pete
sentences.text: No, we don’t.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: All the great storms have names.

sentences.speaker: Pete
sentences.text: No, they don’t.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: I know -- “The Big Snow!”

sentences.speaker: Pete
sentences.text: I am not saying “The Big Snow.”

sentences.speaker: Pete
sentences.text: Welcome to “The Big Snow.”

sentences.speaker: Kelly
sentences.text: The Big Snow broke all kinds of records, didn’t it?

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Yes it did. And every time a record was broken, we celebrated!

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: So far, in Washington, D.C. 29 inches of snow has fallen. That, my dear listeners, is a record! (Honks horn)

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: We just broke the wind speed record! (Honks horn)

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Snow has been falling for 30 hours straight! That’s another record! (Honks horn. Pete comes into room and breaks the horn.)

sentences.speaker: Kelly
sentences.text: By Saturday night, stores and restaurants had closed. Did you bring enough food?

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: I thought I had brought enough food. But I ran out.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Hey, Pete, where is my bag of popcorn?

sentences.speaker: Pete
sentences.text: Maybe you ate it already.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: No, I didn’t.

sentences.speaker: Pete
sentences.text: I haven't seen it. (Pete has popcorn in his beard. Anna tries to hit him.)

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: We had reported together for 48 hours straight!

sentences.speaker: Kelly
sentences.text: Wow. That must have been a great team-building exercise for you and Pete.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Yeah. You - you could say that.

sentences.speaker: Prof. Bot
sentences.text: I hope you found all the sentences with perfect tenses. Learn more on our website!

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Wow. Did you know that bees are dying?

sentences.speaker: Kaveh
sentences.text: That is bad news. If all the bees died, there would be no food. Bees are very important.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Yes, they are. Speaking of bees, one of our little friends is here now.

sentences.speaker: Kaveh
sentences.text: You know, Anna, if you ignore it, it will fly away. But if you swat it, it might sting you.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: I’ll ignore it.  I can ignore it. See, I’m ignoring it. (she is swatting at the bee)

sentences.speaker: Kaveh
sentences.text: Anna, are you afraid of bees?

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: What makes you say that?

sentences.speaker: Kaveh
sentences.text: Anna, you should call my friend, Caroline. She is a beekeeper and a bee educator. If you talk to her, she’ll probably help you get over your fear of bees.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: I am not afraid of bees.

sentences.speaker: Kaveh
sentences.text: Here’s her card.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Ahhh!

sentences.speaker: Prof. Bot
sentences.text: In this lesson, you can learn about conditionals. They have "if" and "will" or "would." There are two kinds of conditional sentences in this lesson.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: I think I'm at the wrong address. This does not look like a place where bees are kept.   ​(knocks on door)

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Oh, sorry to bother you. I’m looking for beekeeper Caroline. I’m here to take her “Learn to Love Bees!” class.

sentences.speaker: Caroline
sentences.text: You’re in the right place! I’m Caroline!

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Oh, nice to meet you! Um, Caroline, I thought this class used real bees and real hives.

sentences.speaker: Caroline
sentences.text: It does! If you look in my backyard, you will see my bees! I’m a home beekeeper!

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: What? You live with bees? That is really amazing! And at the same time really scary.

sentences.speaker: Caroline
sentences.text: It’s not scary. If you come, I’ll show you.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Caroline, how many bees are in that hive?

sentences.speaker: Caroline
sentences.text: About thirty thousand (30,000) in each.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: What? That's amazing! But, aren’t you afraid that they are gonna come out and kill you?

sentences.speaker: Caroline
sentences.text: No, not at all, Anna. Even my children help me. Tell me, why are you afraid of bees?

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: I don't know. Well, when I was a little girl my mom ran out of honey. And I really wanted honey for my pancakes. So, I climbed high into a tree and hit a beehive with a stick … several times. Then I reached inside with my bare hands to pull the honey out. That’s when I got stung … a lot.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Caroline, if you hit a beehive with a stick and reach inside, you might get stung.

sentences.speaker: Caroline
sentences.text: No, Anna. If you do those things, you will get stung.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Yes. I did.

sentences.speaker: Caroline
sentences.text: And you know that it was your fault you got stung, don’t you?

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Yes. I did.

sentences.speaker: Caroline
sentences.text: Bees know your feelings. And if you stay calm, the bees will be calm. If you're nervous, the bees will be nervous. And if bees are nervous, they may sting. So, please be calm.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: I will be calm. I am calm. Okay, I'm ready. I'm ready

sentences.speaker: Caroline
sentences.text: Great. Let’s get our equipment on.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Wait! Wait! I’m not ready! I'm nervous! Give me a minute to be calm.

sentences.speaker: Prof. Bot
sentences.text: Are you ready for one more conditional sentence?

sentences.speaker: Caroline
sentences.text: I have a feeling that your fear of bees will be gone soon. There are things beekeepers do to protect ourselves. For example, we wear protective clothing. This is a beekeeper’s veil, suit and gloves. There are other things we can do, too. If I use a smoker, the bees will stay calm.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Let’s use smoke … lots of smoke.

sentences.speaker: Caroline
sentences.text: Okay, Anna, that’s enough smoke. Another thing you can do is stay calm.  Okay.  When I lift the frame, you will see the bees.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: I’m ready. Let's do this thing!

sentences.speaker: Caroline
sentences.text: Okay, let's put on our protective clothing.

sentences.speaker: Caroline
sentences.text: I will carefully take out a frame. This is where the bees live. There are worker bees, drone bees and the queen bee. The bees have different jobs. The queen bee lays the eggs. The worker bees collect nectar and pollen ​from flowers and bring it back to the hive. Then they make honey!  Now, you hold the frame. There are the bees.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: There are so many! And they are so busy! Now I know why we say, “busy as a bee!”

sentences.speaker: Caroline
sentences.text: Good job, Anna.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Caroline, bees are beautiful and important. If I wanted to help the bees, what would I do?

sentences.speaker: Caroline
sentences.text: Great question. You can plant native flowers that bees like. Here’s a book to help you know which ones to plant.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: It’s a beautiful book. And look, it tells you which bees like which types of flowers.

sentences.speaker: Caroline
sentences.text: It also tells you how the flowers affect the flavor of the honey.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Flowers make a big difference to bees. If they don’t eat, they won’t live.

sentences.speaker: Caroline
sentences.text: Buying local honey also helps the bees. If you want to help bees, do those two things.

sentences.speaker: Prof Bot
sentences.text: I learned a lot about bees. Hey, if I worked with bees, I would not need protective clothing! Guess what? That was a Type 2 conditional.  And I heard a Type 1 conditional, too. (Anna: If they don’t eat, they won’t live.)

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Thanks for the book, Caroline, and the bee puppet and for teaching me about bees. Look … I’m not scared.

sentences.speaker: Caroline
sentences.text: Good job, Anna. If you ever want to see the bees again, I’ll be here! You have my business card. I'll let you see yourself out.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Thanks! Bye! I will plant tons of flowers!

sentences.speaker: Bees
sentences.text: Thanks, Anna. (bees spell out the words)

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Sure thing, bees! Oh, and I'm sorry about hitting that hive when I was a little girl.

sentences.speaker: Bees
sentences.text: We love you, Anna. (bees make a heart sign.)

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Take care, bees! (to herself) Which way is the Metro?

sentences.speaker: Bees
sentences.text: That way. (they draw an arrow)

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Thanks!

sentences.speaker: Prof. Bot
sentences.text: So, if I you want to learn more about bees, visit your local beekeeper like Anna did. Maybe you can try some local honey, too.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Hello! What are you guys looking at?

sentences.speaker: Pete
sentences.text: I’m showing Ashley pictures of my girlfriend. We have so much in common -- even small things. She can’t whistle and I can’t either.

sentences.speaker: Ashley
sentences.text: (to Pete) And here’s a picture of my boyfriend. (sighs)

sentences.speaker: Ashley
sentences.text: My family is big and so is his. I don’t like ball sports and he doesn’t either! (sighs) We are made for each other ...

sentences.speaker: Pete
sentences.text: … and so are we. (sighs)

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Uh… you have found perfect partners … and so have I!

sentences.speaker: Professor Bot
sentences.text: Pete and Ashley are talking about people they love. They are putting two ideas together with connectors.

sentences.speaker: Ashley
sentences.text: You met someone, Anna? That’s great! What’s his name?

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: His name? His name is uh… (stalling, looks around, sees a bus)  Bus … ter.  (stalling, looks around, sees a car)  Car … ter.

sentences.speaker: Ashley
sentences.text: (says it like Anna did) Bus...ter Car...ter?

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: It’s just Buster Carter, Ashley. I like him and he likes me. We’re a great couple.

sentences.speaker: Ashley
sentences.text: Hey, let’s all get dinner tonight, together. You can bring Buster.

sentences.speaker: Pete
sentences.text: (laughing) Yeah, I can’t wait to meet him.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Thanks, Ashley, but he’s really busy tonight with his uh, (looks around, sees squirrel) squirrel collection. Bye, guys! Gotta go!

sentences.speaker: Ashley
sentences.text: Squirrel collection?

sentences.speaker: Pete
sentences.text: You know, she made all that up.

sentences.speaker: Ashley
sentences.text: That’s so sad. She needs to meet someone. Hey, do you know anyone who she might...

sentences.speaker: Pete
sentences.text: No.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: (to herself) Anna, Anna, you lied! You lied! Now, they think you have a boyfriend - with a squirrel collection. Here, squirrel. (throws food) Well, you need to tell them the truth. You don’t have a boyfriend.

sentences.speaker: Man
sentences.text: Excuse me, is this seat taken?

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Ashley, Pete, I need to talk to you. This morning, I lied.

sentences.speaker: Pete
sentences.text: Let me guess. There’s no Buster Carter. What a surprise!

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: I’m sorry. But later I really did meet someone and we have a lot in common!

sentences.speaker: Ashley
sentences.text: He sounds perfect for you, Anna. Can he come tonight?

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: That’s the sad part. You see, he just got a job as a spy, and tonight he leaves on assignment.

sentences.speaker: Pete
sentences.text: Of course he does.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: But that's okay, because now I know that there is someone out there made for me. (looks at the time) Oh, it’s late! I have to see him off at the train station. Bye, you guys!

sentences.speaker: Ashley
sentences.text: Bye Anna! Oh dear, she’s worse than we thought.

sentences.speaker: Pete
sentences.text: She’s lost her mind.

sentences.speaker: Ashley
sentences.text: What should we do?

sentences.speaker: Pete
sentences.text: (happy, excited) Let’s tell her!

sentences.speaker: Ashley
sentences.text: No, Pete. Mr. Right may not be real but he makes her really happy.

sentences.speaker: Professor Bot
sentences.text:
Did you find any other connectors? Notice how the words are in a different order in the part after “so.”  "I am" becomes "am I"  and "he can" becomes "can he." 
"He’s good at flying kites and so am I. I can play the ukulele and so can he."

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Penelope, even though we both love speed walking, could we slow down a bit?

sentences.speaker: Penelope
sentences.text: No way! I think because I’m walking with you, I’m walking faster.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Come on, Penelope. Let's take a break. We've been speed walking since 8 a.m.! You're so competitive! You even wore your medals!

sentences.speaker: Penelope
sentences.text: You brought your trophies! You’re out of shape. When we were little girls, we could speed walk all day! (pulls ahead)

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: (chases her) Hey, wait for me! Hey, you know the speed walking rules! If both feet leave the ground, it’s running! You ran!

sentences.speaker: Prof. Bot
sentences.text: Anna and Penelope are doing something they both love - speed walking!

sentences.speaker: Penelope
sentences.text: Whew! That was great!

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: (Anna catches up) Wow, Penelope, you’re still really fast! Since I’ve been working in an office, my speed walking has been much slower.

sentences.speaker: Penelope
sentences.text: You are slower, Anna. Maybe you should hire a personal trainer.

sentences.speaker: Anna

sentences.text: The words tell and say have similar meanings. But we use them in different ways.

sentences.speaker: Prof Bot
sentences.text: Tell means “to inform or instruct someone with words” and is almost always followed by an indirect object. For example, Sue says, “Tell me about that.”

sentences.speaker: Prof. Bot
sentences.text: The word me is the indirect object and tells us who is being told.

sentences.speaker: Prof. Bot
sentences.text: Say means “to express something with words” and focuses more on the words used. For example, Anna says, “That’s what it said. It said, ‘Use me, Anna.’”

sentences.speaker: Prof. Bot
sentences.text: Listen for when Anna and Sue use tell and say.

sentences.speaker: Sue
sentences.text: Anna, welcome to Decoupage class. Decoupage is just gluing pretty pictures onto stuff.

sentences.speaker: Sue
sentences.text: Anna, I’ve got to talk to this person. I’ll be right back. Don’t start without me.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Got it.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Okay. I can fix this.

sentences.speaker: Sue
sentences.text: Anna, what happened? I told you to wait for me!

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Actually, you told me not to start without you, which I didn’t. Your glue is really sticky.

sentences.speaker: Sue
sentences.text: Next week, let’s try lamp making. There’s – there’s no glue. Here's a flier.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Thanks. See you next week.

sentences.speaker: Sue
sentences.text: Anna, you did really well this week. I think lamp making might be your thing!

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Thanks, Sue. I did everything you told me to do.

sentences.speaker: Sue
sentences.text: Remember: I said to read the instructions really carefully. Where are those instructions?

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Let’s just plug it in!

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: So, what class will you be teaching next week?

sentences.speaker: Prof. Bot
sentences.text: Too bad Anna didn’t follow instructions! Visit our website for more on tell and say!

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Hello?

sentences.speaker: Ms. Weaver
sentences.text: Anna, this is Ms. Weaver.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Ms. Weaver!

sentences.speaker: Ms. Weaver
sentences.text: Tomorrow, you’ll be interviewing musician Emma G.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Emma G?! I will be talking to Emma G?!

sentences.speaker: Ms. Weaver
sentences.text: Anna? Anna, are you there?

sentences.speaker: Professor Bot
sentences.text: Anna and Ms. Weaver used the future continuous verb tense to talk about the interview.

sentences.speaker: Prof. Bot
sentences.text: We use future continuous to talk about actions that will be in progress at or around a time in the future.

sentences.speaker: Prof. Bot
sentences.text: For example, Ms. Weaver says, “Tomorrow, you’ll be interviewing musician Emma G.”

sentences.speaker: Prof. Bot
sentences.text: There are two options for future continuous. The first is: will be + the -ing form of the verb

sentences.speaker: Prof. Bot
sentences.text: And the second is: be + going to be + the -ing form of the verb. Keep watching for more!

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Hello and welcome to The Music! Today, musician Emma G will be joining us here!

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: She is a wonderful songwriter and an amazing singer. And I love her! Let’s give a warm welcome to Emma G!

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Hi. Thank you for coming on the show, Emma G.

sentences.speaker: Emma G
sentences.text: Of course. It’s great to be here.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Well, we can’t wait to hear you sing. I listen to your music a lot. So, I feel like I know you. Is that strange?

sentences.speaker: Emma G
sentences.text: Anna, listening to music can be a very personal experience. So, no, that’s not strange.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Good because I made something for you -- a video scrapbook of our friendship.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: I took photos of you and added myself. I worked on it all weekend.

sentences.speaker: Emma G
sentences.text: Well, that -- that’s strange. Is that even -- is that even legal?

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Now, Emma, let’s talk about your schedule. Tell me ... I mean, tell us exactly where you will be and when. Exactly.

sentences.speaker: Emma G
sentences.text: Sure. Well, in early June, I’ll be performing at several venues across Austin, Texas.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: That’s my vacation week. I can meet you there! We can tour the city. We can have lunch.

sentences.speaker: Emma G
sentences.text: Um, yeah maybe. Then in mid-July, I’m going to be teaching at a music camp in Chicago.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: I’ll be visiting my sister then. She only lives about six hours from Chicago! I could drive over. We could hang out.

sentences.speaker: Emma G
sentences.text: Yeah, uh maybe. You know, maybe now is a good time for some music.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: That’s a great idea. Now, let's hear a song from Emma G.!

sentences.speaker: Emma G
sentences.text: I wrote this song a couple of years ago. It’s called “Wary.”

sentences.speaker: Emma G
sentences.text: Do you believe in happy endings?

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Endings...

sentences.speaker: Emma G
sentences.text: Do you really believe that we could be…

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Be...

sentences.speaker: Emma G
sentences.text: I think something is wrong. I hear a voice in the background.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Sorry. Sorry, Emma. That was me. I’m just so excited.

sentences.speaker: Emma G
sentences.text: No problem. I'm glad you like the song.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: You go ahead. You go ahead.

sentences.speaker: Emma G
sentences.text: Okay. Do you believe in happy endings?

sentences.speaker: Emma G
sentences.text: Anna, there’s no tambourine in this.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: I’m so sorry. I’m so sorry, Emma. See, I’ve always wanted to sing with you.

sentences.speaker: Emma G
sentences.text: Well, come on over then and we can sing a song together first.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: No, I couldn't.

sentences.speaker: Emma G
sentences.text: Come on. It’ll be fun.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Okay! Here. I brought my favorite song.

sentences.speaker: Emma G
sentences.text: Oh, uh okay. Actually, I like this song. Um, are you ready?

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Yes! Yes!

sentences.speaker: Emma G
sentences.text: Okay.

sentences.speaker: ANNA
sentences.text: Hi! I see you like superhero culture. Me too.

sentences.speaker: ANNA
sentences.text: In fact, tonight I’m going to the big superhero convention. Are you going?

sentences.speaker: YOUNG MAN
sentences.text: Um, I don’t know.

sentences.speaker: ANNA
sentences.text: Well, you'd better decide soon. Last year, it sold out.

sentences.speaker: ANNA
sentences.text: So, since we’re talking about superheroes: would you rather become a superhero by accident, like Spiderman, or be born a superhero, like Wonder Woman?

sentences.speaker: ANNA
sentences.text: Take your time. It’s a big question. I thought about it for days –

sentences.speaker: YOUNG MAN
sentences.text: Okay. If I had to choose, I’d rather be born a superhero.

sentences.speaker: ANNA
sentences.text: I’d rather become a superhero by an unexpected accident!

sentences.speaker: YOUNG MAN
sentences.text: Aren’t all accidents unexpected?

sentences.speaker: ANNA
sentences.text: Well, yeah.

sentences.speaker: YOUNG MAN
sentences.text: What was that!? Are you okay?

sentences.speaker: ANNA
sentences.text: I'm better than okay. I feel super!

sentences.speaker: PROF. BOT
sentences.text: Oh No! Anna was just hit by lightning. She had better get help.

sentences.speaker: PROF. BOT
sentences.text: We use had better to give advice. It is very informal and stronger than should and ought to. For example, Anna says: “You'd better decide soon. Last year, it sold out.”

sentences.speaker: PROF. BOT
sentences.text: When we use had better, we usually shorten the word had for personal pronouns.

sentences.speaker: PROF. BOT
sentences.text: We use would rather to say what we or someone else prefers to do or have. For example, the boy says: “Okay. If I had to choose, I’d rather be born a superhero.

sentences.speaker: PROF. BOT
sentences.text: With would rather, we also shorten the word would when used with personal pronouns. Keep watching and listen for had better and would rather.

sentences.speaker: YOUNG MAN
sentences.text: You’d better see a doctor.

sentences.speaker: ANNA
sentences.text: I’ve never felt better!

sentences.speaker: YOUNG MAN
sentences.text: You were just struck by lightning!! And what happened to your hair and your clothes?

sentences.speaker: ANNA
sentences.text: I don't know. Wait, I do know. This is my super suit! And this is my origin story.

sentences.speaker: YOUNG MAN
sentences.text: What are you talking about?

sentences.speaker: ANNA
sentences.text: An origin story tells the beginning of a superhero. You should know that.

sentences.speaker: YOUNG MAN
sentences.text: You're not making any sense, lady.

sentences.speaker: ANNA
sentences.text: I would rather be called Lightning Bolt Lady! It’ll sound great in a theme song: Lightning Bolt Lady!

sentences.speaker: ANNA
sentences.text: Now, I need to find my superpowers --

sentences.speaker: YOUNG MAN
sentences.text: Um, I really think --

sentences.speaker: ANNA
sentences.text: Wait. Don’t tell me. I’ll read your mind. You are thinking you’d like to be my super helper.

sentences.speaker: YOUNG MAN
sentences.text: I was not thinking that.

sentences.speaker: ANNA
sentences.text: ... that you’d like to live in a treehouse.

sentences.speaker: YOUNG MAN
sentences.text: No.

sentences.speaker: ANNA
sentences.text: … that you should eat more vegetables.

sentences.speaker: YOUNG MAN
sentences.text: Please, stop talking. You really should get some help.

sentences.speaker: ANNA
sentences.text: Mind reading is not my superpower. Maybe I can become invisible. I … am … invisible!

sentences.speaker: ANNA
sentences.text: You can’t see me. Who am I? I’m not here. You can’t see me.

sentences.speaker: YOUNG MAN
sentences.text: I can see you and so can everybody else.

sentences.speaker: ANNA
sentences.text: No power of invisibility. Maybe I can create a force field. I feel it working. Nothing can hurt –

sentences.speaker: ANNA
sentences.text: Ow, that wasn’t very nice.  I see I have a lot of work to do. Well, goodbye, non-super person!

sentences.speaker: YOUNG MAN
sentences.text: Wait. I’d better go with you. You might get worse…if that’s even possible.

sentences.speaker: ANNA
sentences.text: That's very nice of you, ordinary human. But I’d rather go by myself. This is a quest.

sentences.speaker: YOUNG MAN
sentences.text: Every time you speak, I get more confused.

sentences.speaker: ANNA
sentences.text: A quest is a part of all superhero stories. You really need to work on your superhero studies. Now, stand back. I’ve never flown before.

sentences.speaker: YOUNG MAN
sentences.text: And you’re not flying now.

sentences.speaker: ANNA
sentences.text: Flying is also not my superpower. That’s too bad. It's going to be expensive to Uber everywhere. You know, I'd rather walk. It’s a nice day. Goodbye, non-super person.

sentences.speaker: YOUNG MAN
sentences.text: I am not talking to strangers again.

sentences.speaker: ANNOUNCER
sentences.text: Will Lightning Bolt Lady find her superpowers … ever? Ouch! Did that brick wall hurt? Will the young man ever talk to a stranger again?

sentences.speaker: ANNOUNCER
sentences.text: Find out on the next episode of Let’s Learn English!

sentences.speaker: ANNOUNCER
sentences.text: When last we saw Anna, she had made a new friend. And they had been talking about superheroes for a while when suddenly Anna became Lightning Bolt Lady!

sentences.speaker: ANNOUNCER
sentences.text: She tried to find her superpowers. But it did not go well.

sentences.speaker: ANNOUNCER
sentences.text: She can’t fly, become invisible or create a force field. And she really cannot walk through walls. Ouch, Lightning Bolt Lady.

sentences.speaker: ANNOUNCER
sentences.text: She had been walking into that wall for about 15 minutes when she had a great idea.

sentences.speaker: LIGHTNING BOLT LADY
sentences.text: I just had a great idea!

sentences.speaker: ANNOUNCER
sentences.text: I can’t wait to hear this one! But first, let’s talk about grammar.

sentences.speaker: ANNOUNCER
sentences.text: Professor Bot is on vacation this week. I’m the announcer. So, I’m going to tell you about the past perfect continuous.

sentences.speaker: ANNOUNCER
sentences.text: We use this verb tense to show that an action started in the past and continued to another time or action in the past.

sentences.speaker: ANNOUNCER
sentences.text: For example, I said, “She had been walking into that wall for about 15 minutes when she had a great idea.”

sentences.speaker: ANNOUNCER
sentences.text: Had been walking is the past perfect continuous of the verb walk. It’s had been plus the -ing form of the verb.

sentences.speaker: ANNOUNCER
sentences.text: You’ll hear me use this verb tense a few more times today.

sentences.speaker: ANNOUNCER
sentences.text: Now, what am I forgetting? Oh right! Lightning Bolt Lady’s great idea.

sentences.speaker: LIGHTNING BOLT LADY
sentences.text: If I want to know my superpowers, I’ll need to learn about lightning!

sentences.speaker: ANNOUNCER
sentences.text: So, she read many books about lightning.

sentences.speaker: LIGHTNING BOLT LADY
sentences.text: Wow. A lightning strike usually lasts less than a second.

sentences.speaker: LIGHTNING BOLT LADY
sentences.text: Lightning is really fast and I like speed walking. So, maybe one of my superpowers is super-speed walking! (to stranger) Bye!

sentences.speaker: LIGHTNING BOLT LADY
sentences.text: Check! Super-speed walking is definitely one of my superpowers.

sentences.speaker: LIGHTNING BOLT LADY
sentences.text: Lightning has millions of volts of electricity. Amazing!

sentences.speaker: ANNOUNCER
sentences.text: She had been looking for hours for someone to help when she found her chance.

sentences.speaker: WOMAN
sentences.text: Hello? Hello? I’m sorry. I’m going to have to call you back. My phone is dying.

sentences.speaker: LIGHTNING BOLT LADY
sentences.text: Excuse me, I can charge your phone.

sentences.speaker: WOMAN
sentences.text: Really? Thanks!

sentences.speaker: LIGHTNING BOLT LADY
sentences.text: I’m Lightning Bolt Lady!

sentences.speaker: ANNOUNCER
sentences.text: She had been practicing her superpowers all day. Suddenly, she heard a terrible sound – a child’s disappointment.

sentences.speaker: ANNOUNCER
sentences.text: These children tried to light a fire for over an hour. But then, they gave up.

sentences.speaker: PARENT
sentences.text: Hey kids, that wood will never burn. It’is too wet.

sentences.speaker: LIGHTNING BOLT LADY
sentences.text: Small humans, what is wrong?

sentences.speaker: CHILD
sentences.text: Stranger danger!

sentences.speaker: LIGHTNING BOLT LADY
sentences.text: I’m Lightning Bolt Lady!

sentences.speaker: YOUNG MAN
sentences.text: Oh no. It’s you.

sentences.speaker: LIGHTNING BOLT LADY
sentences.text: (to YOUNG MAN:) We meet again. And guess what: I found my superpowers.

sentences.speaker: CHILD
sentences.text: Well, we need a fire to toast the marshmallows to make S’mores.

sentences.speaker: LIGHTNING BOLT LADY
sentences.text: I can help.

sentences.speaker: YOUNG MAN
sentences.text: We don’t need a super-speed walker but thanks!

sentences.speaker: LIGHTNING BOLT LADY
sentences.text: Super-speed walking is just one of my superpowers. I can also do this!

sentences.speaker: LIGHTNING BOLT LADY
sentences.text: Sorry! Let me do it again.

sentences.speaker: CHILDREN
sentences.text: Thanks, Lightning Bolt Lady!

sentences.speaker: YOUNG MAN
sentences.text: Lightning Bolt Lady

sentences.speaker: LIGHTNING BOLT LADY
sentences.text: You’re welcome. But you don’t have enough firewood. Using my super-speed walking, I will get more.

sentences.speaker: PARENT
sentences.text: Lightning Bolt Lady, come back! A lightning storm is coming!

sentences.speaker: LIGHTNING BOLT LADY
sentences.text: Not a chance! There’s not a cloud in the …

sentences.speaker: CHILD
sentences.text: Lightning Bolt Lady, are you okay?

sentences.speaker: CHILD
sentences.text: Where's your super-suit?

sentences.speaker: ANNA
sentences.text: Oh no! I've lost my superpowers!

sentences.speaker: YOUNG MAN
sentences.text: It's starting to rain. Do you want to go inside and eat some S’mores?

sentences.speaker: ANNA
sentences.text: You read my mind.

sentences.speaker: ANNA
sentences.text: You know, I thought mind reading would be one of my superpowers. But it wasn’t.

sentences.speaker: CHILD
sentences.text: That’d be a cool superpower.

sentences.speaker: CHILD
sentences.text: But I’d rather be able to talk to animals.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: This article is so interesting. Pete, listen to this: “Somewhere in the world there is someone who looks just like you.”

sentences.speaker: Pete
sentences.text: No one is this handsome.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Oh Pete, there’s something between your teeth.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: (Pete tries to clean his teeth.)

sentences.speaker: Pete
sentences.text: It is gone?

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: No. No. It’s still there. There. You got it. But think of it: There could be two of us in the world!

sentences.speaker: Pete
sentences.text: Two Annas?

sentences.speaker: Pete
sentences.text: Actually, Anna, maybe your silly article is right. Yesterday at work, I met a woman who looks just like you.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Really? Wait, are you making fun of me?

sentences.speaker: Pete
sentences.text: Not this time.

sentences.speaker: Pete
sentences.text: She’s tall and has curly hair. But even her face looks like yours. I think she’s a career consultant.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: I bet she has a lot of great advice. I can’t wait to meet her.

sentences.speaker: Pete
sentences.text: Yes, you can. I met her and she is very difficult.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Pete, she’s just new. We have to give her a chance. What’s her name?

sentences.speaker: Pete
sentences.text: Evelyna or something like that. You can’t miss her. She always wears a hat.

sentences.speaker: Penelope
sentences.text: So, Anna, have you met the new consultant yet?

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: No. But I’ve already heard. We look alike, don’t we?

sentences.speaker: Penelope
sentences.text: Yeah, but you don’t act alike. You’re much nicer than she is.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Maybe she gets nervous at new jobs. Or maybe she’s shy. Let’s not judge, Penelope.

sentences.speaker: Penelope
sentences.text: She’s not nervous or shy. She’s mean.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: You know, we should get to know her better. Let’s invite her to lunch!

sentences.speaker: Penelope
sentences.text: Sorry but I’m busy that day.

sentences.speaker: Penelope
sentences.text: (Penelope walks away. Anna yells after her.)

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Oh, that’s too bad. Hey, I haven’t picked a day yet!

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: (Anna and Pete are playing a game.)

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: This is going to be so much fun. Boy, I can’t wait to play this game.

sentences.speaker: Evilana
sentences.text: How much longer are you going to be?

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: We’ll be just a minute …

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: (Anna turns around and sees her look-alike.)

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: You must be Evelana. I’m Anna. We are look-alikes!

sentences.speaker: Evilana
sentences.text: No, we’re not. And my name is pronounced “Evil-ana.”

sentences.speaker: Pete
sentences.text: Oh. This is going to be fun.

sentences.speaker: Evilana
sentences.text: You had better hurry up. I need this room for a lecture. It’s called: “If You Want to Win, Others Must Lose.” What is all this stuff, anyway?

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: It’s a game. We’re going to play at lunch.

sentences.speaker: Evilana
sentences.text: It’s a stupid child’s game!

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: It’s a fun game. But yes, it is for children.

sentences.speaker: Evilana
sentences.text: Well, you may be childish but I’m not. And you look stupid with that thing on your head.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Well, you look serious with that look on your face. Come on, Pete. Let’s play somewhere else.

sentences.speaker: Pete
sentences.text: Actually, I’m going to stay for Evilana’s lecture.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Fine. You can learn new ways to beat people.

sentences.speaker: Evilana
sentences.text: He will. He will.

sentences.speaker: Evilana
sentences.text: (Days later, Anna and Penelope are playing the game. Pete comes in. He has a problem with his eye.)

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Okay. Am I a food?

sentences.speaker: Penelope
sentences.text: Nope.

sentences.speaker: Pete
sentences.text: Hey, do you guys have room for one more?

sentences.speaker: Penelope
sentences.text: Sure, Pete! Come on over. What happened to your eye?

sentences.speaker: Pete
sentences.text: Evilana “accidentally” hit me. And she didn’t even say sorry. She’s so mean!

sentences.speaker: Penelope
sentences.text: I told you so.

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Here, Pete. Put on this headband. You’ll feel better. Penelope, you’re right. Evilana is an awful person!

sentences.speaker: Penelope
sentences.text: And violent. And now we have to work with her!

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: Haven’t you heard? She’s gone! She was given another assignment.

sentences.speaker: Penelope
sentences.text: What assignment?

sentences.speaker: Anna
sentences.text: I’m not sure. I think it has something to do with outdoors. Anyway, let’s play! Pete it’s your turn.

sentences.speaker: ANNA
sentences.text: Hello, Ms. Weaver!

sentences.speaker: MS. WEAVER
sentences.text: Oh, Anna. I’ve invited some people to dinner Saturday. We’re going to that new seafood restaurant -- Fish on a Dish.

sentences.speaker: MS. WEAVER
sentences.text: Why don’t you join us? My treat.

sentences.speaker: ANNA
sentences.text: Thanks, Ms. Weaver. But I already have plans. My friend has invited me to her houseboat.

sentences.speaker: MS. WEAVER
sentences.text: Houseboat, really? That’s unique.

sentences.speaker: ANNA
sentences.text: Yes, it is. In fact, I’m thinking of living on a houseboat.

sentences.speaker: MS. WEAVER
sentences.text: Aren’t you too tall and klutzy to live on a houseboat?

sentences.speaker: ANNA
sentences.text: I am not too tall!

sentences.speaker: PROF. BOT VO
sentences.text: Is Anna really ready for a houseboat?

sentences.speaker: PROF. BOT
sentences.text: Ms. Weaver invited Anna to dinner. When we make friendly, informal invitations, we use phrases like “Why don’t…?”

sentences.speaker: PROF. BOT
sentences.text: For example, Ms. Weaver said, “Why don’t you join us? My treat!” That’s: Why don’t plus the subject plus the simple form of the verb.

sentences.speaker: PROF. BOT
sentences.text: Anna responded to the invitation by saying, “Thanks, but I already have plans.” Keep watching for more examples of informal invitations!

sentences.speaker: FANNY
sentences.text: Anna, I’m so glad you could come!

sentences.speaker: ANNA
sentences.text: Hi, Fanny!

sentences.speaker: FANNY
sentences.text: Hi, this is my son, Phoenix.

sentences.speaker: ANNA
sentences.text: Hi, Phoenix.

sentences.speaker: FANNY
sentences.text: How about you give Anna a tour and I will make some lunch?

sentences.speaker: PHOENIX
sentences.text: Aye, aye, captain!

sentences.speaker: FANNY
sentences.text: Great!

sentences.speaker: ANNA
sentences.text: Do you really call her “captain”?

sentences.speaker: PHOENIX
sentences.text: I kind of have to.

sentences.speaker: ANNA
sentences.text: So, Phoenix, I think I’d like to live on a houseboat. Do you like living here?

sentences.speaker: PHOENIX
sentences.text: I love it! It’s much different than living in a house.

sentences.speaker: ANNA
sentences.text: Oh, I bet. I bet you had to get rid of a lot of stuff, didn’t you?

sentences.speaker: PHOENIX
sentences.text: No way! We moved from a 3-story house to a boat! So, we really had to downsize!

sentences.speaker: ANNA
sentences.text: I’d have to get rid of a lot of stuff. I have a rock collection and I have some really big rocks.

sentences.speaker: ANNA
sentences.text:
Can you stop this boat from rocking for a minute?

PHOENIX: No. We’re floating on water. I can’t do that.

sentences.speaker: ANNA
sentences.text: Well, since you live on the water, aren’t you afraid of great white sharks?

sentences.speaker: PHOENIX
sentences.text: No, not really. They don’t live in these waters.

sentences.speaker: ANNA

title: Wilbur and Orville Wright: The First Airplane

sentences.text: Wilbur and Orville Wright are the American inventors who made a small engine-powered flying machine.
They proved that flight without the aid of gas-filled balloons was possible.
Wilbur Wright was born in 1867 near Melville, Indiana.
His brother Orville was born four years later in Dayton, Ohio.
As they grew up, the Wright brothers experimented with mechanical things.
Later, the Wright brothers began to design their own flying machine.
They used ideas they had developed from earlier experiments with a toy helicopter, kites, the printing machine and bicycles.
Soon, they needed a place to test their ideas about flight.
The best place with the best wind conditions seemed to be a piece of sandy land in North Carolina along the coast of the Atlantic Ocean.
It was called Kill Devil Hill, near the town of Kitty Hawk.
The Wright brothers did many tests with gliders at Kitty Hawk.
With these tests, they learned how to solve many problems.
By the autumn of 1903, Wilbur and Orville had designed and built an airplane powered by a gasoline engine.
The plane had wings 12 meters across.
It weighed about 340 kilograms, including the pilot.
On December 17th, 1903, they made the world's first flight in a machine that was heavier than air and powered by an engine.
Orville flew the plane 36 meters.
He was in the air for 12 seconds.
The two brothers made three more flights that day.
Four other men watched the Wright brothers' first flights.
One of the men took pictures.
Few newspapers, however, noted the event.
It was almost five years before the Wright brothers became famous.
In 1908, Wilbur went to France.
He gave demonstration flights at heights of 90 meters.
A French company agreed to begin making the Wright brothers' flying machine.
Orville made successful flights in the United States at the time Wilbur was in France.
The United States War Department agreed to buy a Wright brothers' plane.
Wilbur and Orville suddenly became world heroes.
But the brothers were not seeking fame.
They returned to Dayton where they continued to improve their airplanes.
They taught many others how to fly.
Wilbur Wright died of typhoid fever in 1912.
Orville Wright continued designing and inventing until he died many years later, in 1948.
Today, the Wright brothers' first airplane is in the Air and Space Museum in Washington, D.C.
Visitors to the museum can look at the Wright brothers' small plane.
Then they can walk to another area and see space vehicles and a rock collected from the moon.
The world has changed a lot since Wilbur and Orville Wright began the modern age of flight over one hundred years ago.

title: Methods for Protecting Earth against an Asteroid Strike

sentences.text: Astronomers following asteroid activity in space estimate there is a very small chance an object large enough to destroy a whole city could strike Earth in 2032.
But space agency officials say even if such an asteroid keeps heading on a path toward Earth, the world is now much better-equipped to defend itself against such a threat.
The American space agency NASA recently estimated there was a 3.1 percent chance that asteroid 2024 YR4 would hit Earth on December 22, 2032.
That is the highest probability predicted for such a large space rock in modern times.
Richard Moissl is head of the European Space Agency's (ESA) planetary defense office.
While recognizing the risk the asteroid could present, he told the French news agency AFP people should not panic over such predictions.
Astronomers have noted that the more data they gather, the odds of a direct asteroid hit are expected to keep rising over time.
However, scientists say at a certain point the odds will likely drop down to zero.
Moissl said he thinks it is important to remember that even in the unlikely event the probability keeps rising to 100 percent, the world is "not defenseless."
Here are some methods currently being considered as defensive measures to keep humanity safe in case there is a real threat.
Send a spacecraft to hit it Only one planetary defense method has been tried against an asteroid.
In 2022, NASA's Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) sent a spacecraft into the 160-meter-wide Dimorphos asteroid.
The effort successfully changed the asteroid’s orbit around a larger space rock.
Bruce Betts is chief scientist for the nonprofit Planetary Society.
He told AFP that space agencies could hit the 2024 YR4 asteroid with several spacecrafts, observing how each one changed the path.
The asteroid discovered in December is estimated to be 40-90 meters wide -- about half the size of Dimorphos.
"You have to take care not to overdo it," Moissl warned.
He said this is because if a spacecraft only partly destroys an asteroid, it could send smaller pieces of the space rock heading toward Earth.
Non-contact methods A separate idea would involve sending a large spacecraft to fly alongside a threatening asteroid.
The spacecraft would not touch the asteroid, but would use its gravitational force to pull it away from Earth.
Moissl said another non-contact plan would put a spacecraft near the asteroid to eject a continuous flow of atoms to push the asteroid off course.
Scientists have also considered painting one side of the asteroid white.
They believe this could increase the light the object reflects to make it slowly change course.
Contact methods One idea is to use a nuclear weapon against a threatening asteroid.
In laboratory tests, researchers found that X-rays from a nuclear blast could move a rock.
But this is considered more of a plan for kilometers-wide asteroids like the one that killed off the dinosaurs.
And this method also carries the risk that a nuclear explosion could send additional pieces of the asteroid falling toward Earth.
A similar method – but one considered less dangerous – would involve shooting laser beams from a spacecraft to destroy the side of an asteroid in an effort to push it away from Earth.
If all else fails Moissl said that if all else fails, at least the world will have a good idea where a threatening asteroid would strike.
Since astronomers believe most asteroids would at most threaten to destroy one city, efforts could be organized to get people out of an area before a strike.
"Seven-and-a-half years is a long time to prepare," Moissl added.
He also noted that even with the rising odds involving 2024 YR4, there is still about a 97 percent chance the asteroid will miss Earth.

title: Total Lunar Eclipse to Turn Moon Red

sentences.text: A total lunar eclipse is about to make the moon appear a reddish color across the Western Hemisphere.
The event will happen Thursday night into Friday morning.
The best places to see the eclipse will be in North America and South America.
Parts of Africa and Europe may also get brief views.
A lunar eclipse happens when the sun, Earth, and moon line up just right, with Earth positioned between the sun and moon.
This causes the Earth to create a shadow on the moon.
In a total lunar eclipse, the Earth’s shadow covers all of the moon.
Another kind of eclipse is a solar eclipse.
In a solar eclipse, the moon gets in a position where it blocks light from the sun, causing a partial or full shadow on Earth.
A total lunar eclipse can also be called a blood moon.
It makes the moon appear reddish-orange, similar to the element copper.
The color comes from small amounts of sunlight passing through the Earth’s atmosphere.
The American space agency NASA says lunar and solar eclipses happen between four and seven times a year.
The last total lunar eclipse was in 2022.
This one will be visible for about one hour starting Friday morning at 2:26 a.m. Eastern Daylight Time (EDT).
The time when the Earth’s shadow covers all of the moon will be close to 3 a.m. EDT.
“As long as the sky is clear, you should be able to see it,” Shannon Schmoll told the Associated Press.
She is the director of Abrams Planetarium at Michigan State University.
No special equipment will be needed to see the reddish moon.
The total lunar eclipse may be harder to see in Europe and Africa because the moon will be close to setting.
Michael Faison is an astronomy expert from Yale University.
He told the AP, “This is really an eclipse for North and South America.”
Zoe Ortiz is a historian with the University of North Texas.
She noted that different civilizations have observed lunar eclipses for thousands of years.
This helped ancient people learn things about the behaviors of the sun, moon, and stars.
“They were looking at the night sky and they had a much brighter vision than we do today,” Ortiz said.
The ancient Greek thinker and writer Aristotle observed that Earths’ shadow on the moon during a lunar eclipse was always curved.
This fact supported proof that the Earth is round.
The next total lunar eclipse will appear in the sky September 7, across parts of Asia, Africa, Australia and Europe.
Parts of the Americas will get the next chance to see one in March 2026.

title: Study Shows How Earth’s Orbit Affects Ice Ages

sentences.text: A recent study suggests the next ice age will likely begin in about 11,000 years unless emissions change the effects of natural climate cycles.
An ice age is a period of reduced temperatures causing ice to cover large areas of the northern and southern parts of the world.
A group of scientists studied changes in the shape of the Earth’s orbit around the sun, the tilt of the Earth’s axis and the movement of the axis itself, called a wobble.
These three motions are believed to happen in cycles.
The Serbian scientist Milutin Milankovitch developed a theory about 100 years ago that these cycles affected Earth’s long-term climate.
The team noted that small changes in Earth’s orbit around the Sun caused predictable cycles of warming and cooling over a period of about 100,000 years.
These findings permitted the team to determine how the three factors of tilt, wobble, and the shape of Earth's orbit might have affected the Earth’s climate over the last 900,000 years.
The scientists examined a million-year record of climate by looking at ice sheets across the northern half of the world and deep ocean temperatures.
They then compared this data with small but regular changes in Earth’s orbit over time.
The lead writer of the study is Stephen Barker, a professor at Cardiff University in Britain.

He told the French News Agency (AFP) that for many years it has been difficult for scientists to show exactly how small changes in Earth’s orbit have led to huge changes between warm and cold periods.
Earth is believed to go through cycles of ice ages and warm periods.
The last ice age is thought to have ended around 11,700 years ago.
Scientists, such as Milankovitch, have long seen a connection between Earth's orbit and climate.
However, researchers have struggled to precisely date when each of the climate changes happened.
It has also been difficult for them to know exactly which orbit positions affect the start and stop of cold or warm periods.
Barker said his team of researchers studied slow changes in temperature over long periods of time instead of only looking at shorter periods of change between cold and warm climates.
Barker told AFP, "We would expect a glaciation to occur within the next 11,000 years, and it would end in 66,000 years' time."
Lorraine Lisiecki is a professor at the University of California, Santa Barbara, and a co-writer of the study.
She said the study shows that changes in climate over tens of thousands of years are not random.
The team aims to expand its findings to investigate the long-term effects of human activity on climate.
They also want to find out how it might affect Earth’s natural climate cycles.

title: A Short History of Spacecraft Landings on the Moon

sentences.text: Many years have passed since the first spacecraft landed on the moon in 1966.
From then until now, there have been many additional attempts with some succeeding and others failing.
Here is a short history of some of these attempts.
First victories The Soviet Union’s Luna 9 spacecraft was the first to land on the moon.
It touched down on the lunar surface in 1966.
The landing came after several other Soviet spacecraft either did not reach the moon or crashed on the surface.
The American space agency NASA says Luna 9 was the first spacecraft to carry out a soft landing on the moon.
It was also the first to send “photographic data” from the moon’s surface to Earth.
Luna 9’s landing proved “the lunar surface could support the weight of a lander and that an object would not sink into a loose layer of dust as some models predicted,” NASA said.
In May 1966, the United States followed with its Surveyor 1 mission.

NASA describes this effort as “the first of a series of seven robotic spacecraft sent to the moon to gather data in preparation for NASA's Apollo missions.” The successful soft landing of Surveyor 1 “was one of the great successes of NASA's early lunar and interplanetary program.”
Both the U.S. and Soviet Union had other successful robotic landings.
Next, the countries aimed to be the first to land humans on the moon.
Apollo program In 1969, NASA successfully landed Apollo 11 astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin on the moon.
The U.S. Apollo program sent 12 astronauts to explore the moon over six missions.
Apollo 17 was the last in 1972.
The U.S. is still the only country to land humans on the moon.
NASA officials say the agency’s Artemis program aims to return astronauts to the lunar surface possibly by the end of 2026.
China expands space efforts In 2013, China became the third country to successfully land a spacecraft on the moon.
China landed an exploring vehicle, or rover named Yutu that year.
China followed with the Yutu-2 rover in 2019, this time touching down on the moon’s unexplored far side.
In 2020, China successfully returned samples of rock and dirt collected by the rovers.
The mission returned about 1.7 kilograms of lunar material collected from the near side of the moon.
Then in 2024, another mission returned rock and soil samples from the less explored far side of the moon.
China has said it aims to land its astronauts on the moon by 2030.
Russian landing failure In 2023, Russia tried its first moon landing in nearly 50 years.
The Luna 25 spacecraft was attempting to land near the lunar south pole.
But it is believed to have crash landed on the moon’s surface.
The country’s last effort before that, Luna 24 in 1976, landed successfully and returned moon rocks to Earth.
India succeeds on second attempt After its first lander crashed into the moon in 2019, India made its second attempt in 2023.
The country successfully landed its Chandrayaan-3 spacecraft on the lunar surface.
The mission made India the fourth nation to complete a moon landing.
Japan lands sideways In January 2024, Japan became the fifth country to successfully land a spacecraft on the moon.
But the SLIM spacecraft landed upside down.
This caused some power and communication problems, but the lander was able to operate for a short time.

title: Scientists Link Gene to Human Speech

sentences.text: A new study suggests the beginnings of human speech are linked to genetics.
The research identifies a protein – found only in people – that may have helped early humans develop spoken communication.
Scientists involved in the study say this new speaking ability became important for humans’ survival.
For example, speech permitted individuals to share information, organize activities and pass down knowledge.
These abilities are now seen as an advantage humans had over their relatives, such as the Neanderthals and Denisovans.
The researchers recently published their findings in a study in the journal Nature Communications.
Liza Finestack teaches about speech and hearing at the University of Minnesota.
She told The Associated Press (AP) the new study is "a good first step to start looking at the specific genes" that may affect speech and language development.
Finestack was not involved in the study.
Dr. Robert Darnell has long been studying the protein – called NOVA1 – at his laboratory at New York’s Rockefeller University.
He helped lead the new research and was a writer of the study.
Darnell told the AP the genetic version, or variant, included the protein that helped humans develop into the “dominant species” that remains today.
The latest research involved scientists using CRISPR gene editing methods to replace the NOVA1 protein found in mice with the one found in humans.
The aim was to test the real-life effects of the genetic variant.
The researchers were surprised to learn that the variant changed the way the animals called out to each other.
Baby mice with the human variant made a different sound than normal mice do when their mother came around.
Adult male mice with the variant also made different sounds when they were near a female they wanted to mate with.
Darnell said both of these situations gave the mice a reason to speak.
Those with the human variant "spoke differently," demonstrating the gene’s influence in speech, he added.
This is not the first time a gene has been linked to speech.
In 2001, British scientists said they had discovered the first gene tied to a language and speech disorder.
Researchers called this human language gene FOXP2.
But even though FOXP2 was found to be linked to human language, the variant in modern humans was not found in our species alone.
Later research found it was shared with Neanderthals.
The NOVA1 variant in modern humans, on the other hand, is found only in our species, Darnell said.
The presence of a gene variant is not the only thing that permits people to speak.
The ability also depends on physical elements in the human throat and areas of the brain that work together to help people produce speech and understand language.
Darnell said he hopes the recent work can lead to new ways to treat speech-related problems.
The University of Minnesota's Finestack noted the genetic findings could also one day permit scientists to identify people who might need help developing speech and language early in life.

title: Private Lander Carrying NASA Experiments Lands on the Moon

sentences.text: A private spacecraft carrying several science experiments has successfully landed on the moon.
The lander, called Blue Ghost, was built by the American company Firefly Aerospace.
The spacecraft touched down March 2 on the part of the moon’s near side called Mare Crisium.
The near side of the moon is the side facing Earth.
Officials at Firefly’s Mission Control center near Austin, Texas, confirmed the successful landing.
The chief engineer for the Blue Ghost mission, Will Coogan, announced to excited workers: “We’re on the moon.”
The officials said the spacecraft landed in the right position and was operating normally.
The successful touchdown makes Firefly the first private company to land a spacecraft on the moon without crashing or having a major problem.
Only five countries can claim successful moon landings: Russia, the United States, China, India and Japan.
Blue Ghost is named after a rare kind of firefly found in the U.S. The four-legged lander is two meters tall and 3.5 meters wide.
It launched in mid-January from Florida, carrying 10 experiments for the American space agency NASA.
In a statement, NASA said the 10 experiments are designed to operate on the surface of the moon for one lunar day, which is about 14 Earth days.
The Associated Press reported that NASA paid $101 million for the spacecraft and $44 million for the equipment it carried.
It was the third mission under NASA’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) program.
The program aims to turn over the country’s major space missions to private companies to reduce costs.
Several other companies are part of the program.
Another lander, called Athena, is set to attempt a moon landing on March 6.
That four-meter-tall spacecraft was built and operated by Houston-based Intuitive Machines.
It will land on another part of the moon, about 160 kilometers from the lunar south pole.
A third lander from private Japanese company ispace will attempt a moon landing in about three months.
The lander, called Resilience, shared its rocket ride with Blue Ghost.
But it took a longer path to the moon.
The company is also attempting to land on the moon for the second time.
Its first lander crashed in 2023.
NASA has said it aims to have two private landers launch to the moon each year, realizing some missions will fail.
The space agency’s top science officer is Nicky Fox.
She told the AP the latest launches “open up a whole new way for us to get more science to space and to the moon."
In the past, NASA’s successful moon landings involving astronauts cost billions of dollars.
But Firefly chief Jason Kim said the private companies now building and launching spacecraft have a limited budget and the spacecraft operate robotically.
Kim said everything went just as planned with Blue Ghost’s landing.
“We got some moon dust on our boots," he added.

title: New Discovery Could Explain What Gives Mars its Red Color

sentences.text: Scientists say they might have identified the mineral on Mars that is responsible for making the planet appear red.
New data collected on Mars through several methods suggests the substance, called ferrihydrite, is likely found in dust and rock material across wide areas of the planet.
The team carrying out the research describes ferrihydrite as an “iron oxide mineral.”
The mineral appears reddish in color and can form in water-rich environments.
The scientists said discovering large amounts of it on Mars adds to existing evidence that the planet might have held a large supply of liquid water in the past.
The research was carried out by an international team led by America’s Brown University and the University of Bern in Switzerland.
The findings recently appeared in a study published in Nature Communications.
The researchers noted that scientists have long wondered about the exact substance that gives Mars – which is also known as the Red Planet – its deep red color.
Past studies had suggested a mineral called hematite might be the cause.
The study is based on Martian data collected by several spacecraft.
These include the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, operated by the American space agency NASA.
In addition, information was captured by instruments aboard the European Space Agency’s (ESA's) Mars Express and Trace Gas orbiters.
Some data also came from exploring vehicles, called rovers, operating on Mars.
In their examinations, the researchers also used manmade, or synthetic, material designed to look and feel similar to real Martian dust.
Adomas Valantinas currently works as a researcher at Brown University’s Department of Earth, Environment & Planetary Sciences.
He helped write the study.
Valantinas noted the mystery of why Mars is red had been considered “for hundreds, if not thousands, of years.”
Valantinas recognized his team was not the first to consider ferrihydrite as a possible reason for the coloring of Mars.
But he noted, “it has never been proven as we have now, using observational data and novel laboratory methods…”
Valantinas noted the discovery of widespread ferrihydrite suggests Mars once held liquid water that would have made it possible for the planet to support some form of life.
"Our study reveals that ferrihydrite formation on Mars required the presence of both oxygen…and water capable of reacting with iron,” he added.
“These conditions were very different from the dry, cold environment of Mars today."
John Mustard is a planetary expert at Brown University and was a co-writer of the study.
He called it “a door-opening opportunity” for future research.
But he added that additional study is needed to confirm the team’s latest findings.
"As exciting as the new findings are, we realize that our results can only be verified by samples from Mars, which are currently being collected by NASA's Perseverance rover,” Mustard said.
He added, “When we get those back, we will be able to check whether our theory about ferrihydrite is correct."

title: Scientists Discover Stonehenge-like Circle in Denmark

sentences.text: Danish researchers have announced the discovery of a collection of wooden pieces placed in a circle that are believed to date back thousands of years ago.
The team says the wood pieces and some other objects were found during building work in the northwestern Danish town of Aars.
The discovery led the researchers to suggest the people who placed the wooden pieces might have been linked to a group who built Britain’s famous Stonehenge stone structure.
A total of 45 ancient wood pieces were discovered underground last week during building, or construction, work.
The pieces formed a circle about 30 meters across.
In an email to the French news agency AFP, Sidsel Wahlin of the town’s Vesthimmerlands museum described the discovery as “a once in a lifetime find.”
The circle "points to a strong connection with the British henge world," she added.
The British Museum says on its website the first stones placed at Stonehenge, in southern England, are believed to have started arriving there around 3000 BC.
The Danish researchers said they were also looking to see whether an inner circle might also exist where the wooden pieces were found.
Wahlin noted that in the past, other wood circles had been found on the Danish island of Bornholm in the Baltic Sea.
But Wahlin said the circle in Aars was "the first one of this larger type that we can properly investigate.”
Archeologists working at the building site also found an ancient settlement that included a leader’s grave and a bronze sword.
Wahlin said her team was still carrying out detailed work in the area in an effort to estimate the age and purpose of the materials.
In particular, the archeologists are now searching for religious-connected materials known as "ritual deposits." These might include flint arrow heads and small knives or daggers.
Wahlin said the researchers will continue looking for links between the Aars site and other groups, such as those who built Stonehenge.
She added the influence of other groups had already been found in some objects and graves found in Denmark.

title: The Planets Gather for a Show in the Evening Sky

sentences.text: All seven major planets form a kind of parade in the sky at the end of February.
Although two of the planets are not visible to the unaided eye, all are on the same side of the sun during the evening hours.
This planetary grouping happens when the planets appear to line up in the night sky as seen from Earth.
They do not form a straight line, but they do stretch across the evening sky this year.
The American space agency, NASA, says these astronomical gatherings are common.
A parade of four or five planets visible to the unaided eye happens every few years.
A similar parade took place last June, but only two planets could be seen without the use of special equipment.
Six planets were visible in January.
Four were visible to the unaided eye.
In recent weeks, Mercury joined the group.
Venus, Mars and Jupiter are all easily visible in the evening.
Saturn is now very close to the setting sun and Mercury is close to the horizon, making both hard to see.
Uranus and Neptune are the most distant planets.
